blocks.x: I was the founder of the Festival of Flowers, which is an annual affair that they still have going on. Then I wrote the Sugar Bowl Parade and then I was at the Sanger Theatre. I was 24 years old and I did that and played the first notes for the first time on several, on two New Orleans TV stations. WDSU, when they went NBC, I was the first note to hit it on a timpani and the first note to hit a chime on WWL when they went on the air. As the president of a National Rental Association, I was probably not for two years and I spoke before different organizations on the subjects. I did the Colgate Hour with Peggy Lee and I can't remember, the captain of Tennille, the captain is his. He was a conductor of San Francisco Symphony. I can't think of his name.
What did he do? He was the son of. The son of the conductor of that. I can't think of his name right now.
Then I was with Huey Long with his band when we used to do broadcasts. Did I tell you about the March of Dimes thing at the, at the, at the, at the, at the, uh, municipal auditorium?
Not that I remember. You only talked about the Sam of Pops.

This was the first March of Dimes when Roosevelt was alive. It was the March of Dimes was set up in his honor because of his, his affliction and his polioids. And it was there with Lou Forbes. He was, we were at the Roseville Hotel then. And they had, on stage, they had a regular backdrop on it. And Lou Forbes was conducting, and then we got a normal applause hand after we were finished playing. And as we were getting off the stage for the next band, our show actor was coming on, it started a tremendous amount of applause. So Lou Forbes goes and gets the band, come on back on the stage and take a bow. Stand in front. And Lou Forbes was standing up there bowing. But he overlooked one thing. We were not facing the back of the stage. In the back of the stage, there was a red big American flag and a big picture of Franklin Roosevelt. And they're putting for the flag in Roosevelt's picture. And we're out there taking bows. Dummies. That's a, that was funny. Kurt, can you tell me your real name? My real name? Yes.
Yes. My real name is Curtis D. Jerdy. Okay.
I just want to see that it was picking him up.
And you're, and you're a Godfrey?
Mayor Hirsch. Yeah. And I'm not sure.
I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure. I'm not sure.
I'm not sure. Mayor Hirsch.
Yeah. And my name is Dick Allen.
I think it's picking up something. Oh, I forgot. What's today's date?
Today is one day before the signing of the Armistice of World War I. And 19...
18. Yeah.
And this is 1987.
Yeah. So yeah. November 10th, 1987. November 11th.
Today's the 10th. So it's all, almost 70 years. Like a year and a day.
Down there. Sir? Down there then. Yeah. Down there. A year and a day.
Yeah.
Yeah.
November the 10th. Today. Yeah. Okay. We've got that. And when you're home on Marshall... Marshall Foch. Foch. Yeah.
Named after the famous French general, Marshall. All of the streets in Lakeview are named after World War I.

Uh-huh. You have Argonne. No, Argonne was World War II, wasn't it? No, that was one. I think my father was saying. Was that one? Argonne was World War I. You have Marshall Foch, General Diaz, General Haig, and... Where's Mouton? Mouton is over... Oh, I'll find her over there. It's across the street. Yeah. Yeah. You have Argonne. No, Argonne was World War II, wasn't it? No, that was one. Was that one?
The thing my father was saying.
Argonne was World War I. You have Marshall Foch, General Diaz, General Haig, and... That's it. Where's Mouton? Mouton is over...
Oh, I'll find her over there.
Yeah. It's across the street. It's not a parallel to Canal Boulevard. I wanted to ask you when you left Greenwood. Greenville. Greenville? Yeah. Why did I say that?
I know better.
Well, it was up in Mississippi.
I left Greenville when I was about... Maybe a year old.
Because we were out...
We were living on South Scott Street in 1911.

So I was born in Seven. And maybe I left Greenville when I was about... Maybe a year old. Because we were out... We were living on South Scott Street in 1911. So I was born in Seven. And maybe I left Greenville when I was about... Yeah, maybe one year or a year and a half old. Because we lived down on Frenchman Street. Was born down on Frenchman Street. And my sister, who was two years younger than I was... Was born down on Frenchman Street. On Frenchman of Decatur. On the third floor. on the third floor, the front room. That must have been a wonderful thing for my mother, to haul two kids up two flights of stairs with the toilet down on the first floor.
How do you spell Rougelot?

Rougelot. Rougelot. R-O-U-G-E-L-O-T. That was a famous... That was a famous... department store. They sold everything. It was like D.H. Holmes or Maison Blanche, or similar to that. It was the biggest store down there. The thing about Frenchman Street, getting into that, there was a street that had everything on it. They had a fire department, they had a bank, they had bakeries, they had general merchandise stores, shoe stores, barbershops, everything that you... Actually, a library, a public library. Had everything within... within three blocks.
What about Washington Square?

Washington Square. It was... It was still a square, playground-like. They've discontinued the playground department of it, since they've... They've redone the thing. The Washington Square was... in later years... by the city, and they put this fence around it. They never had a fence before. They used to play football. And they used... The kids used to get in there and had basketball courts and things like that.
I don't think I ever went to a concert there.
Huh?
I don't think I ever went to a concert there.

They had baseball and everything. I don't think they had a concert, any kind of concerts there. It was not a high-class neighborhood in those days. It was... It was an Italian neighborhood. I mean, a low-class...
Uh-huh.

Low-class neighborhood and a bunch of kids there. Either thieves, stealing off of trains going by there. You had... The L&N Railroad was coming right back of it on Elysian Fields. And... What they had done in the past year, they've fenced it in and they put flowers and shrubbery and everything in there. They made a beautiful park. In fact, the Frenchman Street merchants put up a lot of money to really refurbish the square before they refurbished it. And there was a plaque up there, a bronze plaque that they had up there with the mayor, the offices of the city, like the mayor and the commission council on that one place. Uh-huh. And on the other plaque, they had the names of the Frenchman Street merchants who donated to refurbishing the condition before they re-refurbished it. And my father's name was... I tried to get the... I tried to get that after they tore it down and they told me that they didn't know what the hell they did with it. And I went over to Ricker's to see if they had it, I would have bought it. Because I hadn't had all the names of the different... all the names of the different merchants on Frenchman Street that put up money to help to refurbish it. Uh-huh. But I couldn't find it. Never could find it.
You went to... Is that Ricker and La Rocca's?

No, Ricker... They buy... They tear down buildings and they... Demolition. Demolition people, yeah. Yeah. They have... They've done very well in the past few years, especially with tearing down the old buildings that... Today, with reconstituting the old buildings and so forth, there's a lot of stuff over there that they reuse that they buy... that people can buy to put into their buildings now. Give you that. The... The Maroney effect. Oh, yeah. That's... Yeah, we used to call it
Little Andola.
I love when they... They give you the name of a... Italianate... Italianate design. We used to call them shotgun houses.
Yeah.

You know why they call them shotgun houses? Do you know? I've always assumed because of the... the barrel effect. No, you can say at the front door with a shotgun it shoots right through to the back door. There's nothing in between. There's a door all the way going... going all the way back. And that's what... What they call the shotgun... But they've got different names by now. They're finding out more people... That wasn't nothing... A bunch of thieves and they're glorifying them. It's a funny thing how history has a... In fact, I'm reading... I'm reading Buddy Stahl's book on New Orleans. You know how they... They got different things in there how people didn't know how... what they're saying and they're saying it... And it's... It's very logical what they're saying. But it's funny. It's a funny darn thing how the word banker... how the word... how the name of craps... dice... got to be called the name of craps. It used to be called chances. That's what the original name of craps was chances. And I read that... there's all kind of... all kind of things.
How did it come to be called craps? Yeah. How did it come to be called craps?
Because of the sound. It sounded like something... cracking.
Really?
Cracking like that. With the dice in your hand with the... rolling the dice. You're right? You're... what you're doing?
I'm writing your name down here so in case we... get the boxes mixed up. Okay. You know...
which real as it is...
Do you know the name Lewis Hirsch? Lewis A. Hirsch? Have you ever heard of that?
No.
He was in the music business and that's all I know about him. I don't know what about him. I'll give you something
to make it easier.
Okay. Now you got it stuck on. You gotta lick it.
Okay. In the moment, in case you need it. Oh, we will.
How's that? Gonna be running out of tape. How's that? Yeah, that's fine. That's got the real stuff on it.
All right. What do you consider your more important influences in music, Godfrey?

That's hard to answer. I was influenced by Philip Gordon who was a concert pianist. But I mean, during my early days, I mean, I couldn't, I didn't get, I really didn't get around like a lot of these guys did. I was, I was always an uptown boy. I never was downtown. Those that lived like back of town and things in it, they were in a different environment than we were up in the university section. I mean, we didn't, we didn't really go for that particular environment. And you didn't get the chance. I mean, like they tell me about playing in houses of ill repute and things like that. Well, I mean, it wasn't until we were 18 years old that we knew what they were. and the funny thing about it, when one of the young players just about that age of senility that I found it necessary. Instead of raping some young lady, it was cheaper to spend a dollar or two dollars to go down to the district. And we used to go down there, Louie Macinda, Maya Weinberg, Jake Ansberg, and myself. It was four of us. We were in the same band. Making about five dollars at the most or four dollars or three dollars at the night, we'd go down there at the Stag Hotel. And there was a room down there. It was all mirrors and they had a piano in there. And we used to go in there maybe about two o'clock in the morning when things were quiet and we'd play music for them. And they'd start dancing and we'd dance, they'd dance together and we'd dance with them. And after a half hour or so, we'd all disappear to different rooms for a little sex. And that was, that didn't have any great impression on me except that it was fun. And it was cheaper. It was cheaper than getting involved with some dame and supporting her for the rest of your life when you were about time to have a little fun. And this is a problem with today. I mean, I mean, I think today, I mean, kids get too involved too young and it doesn't last. I think if they could satisfy themselves other than the girl that said, now, honey, I'm pregnant, that's it. But, I never did get involved too much. In fact, believe it or not, I never did play with a colored musician in New Orleans.
Really?

Never. Never did sit in with a colored musician. Oddly enough, when I first, when I went to California with Louis Prima in 1937, we had a piano player, I don't remember his name, but he was a great piano, relief piano player. And we'd get on the stand to play while he was, and Louis would say, keep on playing. He said, you and Louis, because Frank Venera wasn't the greatest pianist in the world for jazz. And Louis would let him play with us and get the band on and say, believe me, that was the first colored fellow that I ever played with, and I felt like a, like a woman losing her virginity, playing with a colored man for the first time. Believe me, you didn't, you didn't do those things in New Orleans. Do you remember anything like that?
Well, I can remember that, sure, up into the 60s or so, not a problem with anybody who tried to do that. Well, the funniest thing

that ever happened in my life, I'm glad to know that it was 11.30 or 12 o'clock at night. When Duke Ellington, I knew the Duke Ellington band, I knew every guy in the band, because we worked together in New York. I mean, they were upstairs, we were downstairs, we were not in the same band, but every intermission we were together, and Sonny Greer was a dear friend of mine, the drummer, and Roy Eldridge, I knew Roy very well, and they came down here and they played, that's when I first came home, about 1941 or 42, when I came home, before, just before I went into service, 42, and they had a concert at Booker T. Washington Auditorium, and, it was, it was, before I went into service, I went into service in 43, yeah, about 42, I went, they had a concert at the Booker T. Washington Auditorium, and I was gonna go to it, I didn't have a date or anything like that, so I got a fifth of booze, and I went, I got down there a little early, and I went backstage, oh, I went and bought my ticket first, so the best ticket in the house was five dollars, which is in the front rows, downstairs, the orchestra, and it went up to two dollars in the back, figuring that, buying a five dollar ticket, I wouldn't be involved too much with, with black people down in the front, so I went backstage, and they gave them a bottle, and before everybody was having a drink, I even had qualms about drinking out of the same bottle as I called it for all of you, so I, we had a drink, and then after the show was over, I told Senator, oh, well, I had my car, I said, come on, I'll drive you down to this railroad station, you want to go out, anybody else want, yeah, get Sonny, so we got Sonny Greer, and, and the drummer, Sonny, and, the drummer, not Sonny Greer, not, Sonny Greer's the name of the drummer, who's the first alto man?
Johnny Hodges?

Johnny Hodges, Johnny Hodges, Johnny, Johnny Hodges and Sonny came with me, and what, so, Sonny always had an affectionate way of walking with you, put his arm around you and he's walking like this and always, even in New York, he used to take me up to Harlem and what, I knew more about Harlem than I knew about Bourbon Street because Sonny used to take me up there and O'Neal Spenter used to take me up there and he used to go up there to get ribs and it was like walking in, in your own living room, you know, you were not scared or nothing and, so we get down to the, get down to the L&N station and park the car and there's Sonny and they're loading up the train right there into the station and they're putting in all the instruments and there's Duke standing there helping to put the instruments in and getting rearranged and so forth. He's walking there,
Duke, Duke, look who's here, look, Son Godfrey's here, Godfrey's here.

I said, Jesus, if somebody sees me with this, I said, I'll be ostracized in New Orleans. Well, it was around 1130, 1230 at 12 o'clock at night and nobody was down there in the railroad station because this was a special train that they had and they were just loading it up there and I saw the guys and I knew the whole band. It was, it was a great gang of guys Ben Webster and the trombone player that wrote Perdido and the whole gang. Was Otto Hardwick
in the band?
Who?
Otto Hardwick.
He played alto too. Probably, probably, probably third, third, sixth, third.
I can't remember how.

He was, it was a great, it was a great band and we were very close and then they went away but nothing happened. I mean, I'll tell you, I was so afraid somebody was going to see me with a nigger walking around with his arm around my shoulder but Sonny, when I told Sonny, my father died, he absolutely cried because even when Duke Ellington used to come down to the auditorium, oh, I got to tell you this, when I went back to my seat, the five dollar seats, thinking there were going to be all rich, white people sitting in the five dollar seats, the white people, rich people were sitting in the two dollar seats in the back and all of them in the front was all black. They got the five dollar seats but Juan Tizzo was a trombone player and they were all a beautiful bunch of guys. Well, you see, we were down at Jack Dempsey's and they were playing up at the Paradise Restaurant right above us. It was right on the second floor above Jack Dempsey's in the Brill Building. And uh, no it wasn't the Brill Building, it was down, right next to the Brill Building. But uh, the Duke was a gentleman, he was a real gentleman, this guy. And uh, the guys, all the guys were gentlemen. There was nothing wrong with them. And uh, Duke's band, Duke's band was, and his son took over the band and it was nothing like what it used to be. The closest thing to Duke Ellington's band that I have ever heard, I mean Duke Ellington's good band, that I ever heard, was when Woody Herman was down here at the Hyatt Regency Hotel. He had a hell of a band down here. And there was only one trouble with it. It was too good and it was too loud and the damn women didn't understand it, cause my own wife, they had a whole Dixieland band there, with half-assed musicians playing and playing not too loud. I said, which one did you like? Oh, I like the Dixieland band better. I said, why? She said, the other band was too loud, couldn't appreciate it. But I mean, that band that they had down here, he had about five trumpet players with him. And Woody had one hell of a band down here at the, did you get a chance to hear him with the Hyatt Regency down there? Yeah. What was your opinion of it? Well, I thought it was, he had a good
band, but they were a little inconsistent, depending, you know, if you caught him on a good night. That's probably a good night. I thought it was a good night evidently. But I mean, it was, it was

a hell of a band. That's, but it was the closest thing to, to, to, to, uh, Ellington that I ever heard. You knew Ben Pollock, huh? I'd met Ben Pollock. I didn't know him personally. I've, I've, I've, I've, I've I've, I know that, I've, I've met him several times. I never knew Ben personally. I knew Gene Krupa, I knew Gene personally. Did you like the way Ben Pollock played? Yeah. He had, he was a, he was a, he had a different style of most, he was a, he was a, he was a great brush player. He used to play brushes on the bass drum. He played one hand on the bass drum with a brush, with one hand on the snare drum with a brush. And he, he, he was, he, he was a good steady drummer. He was not a, a flashy drummer. He, he had a, a great amount of rhythm in his drums. And didn't, he wasn't, he wasn't a Gene Krupa. I mean Gene was, uh, and Gene to me, was not the greatest drummer in the world. He had a personality of how to show off. He could make you look that, make you think that he was doing something. But in my opinion, I mean Gene was, I, I know a lot of drummers technically, who, who, there was one guy by the name of Nat Sadler from New York, who I got a job for him with Russ Morgan's band. I knew Russ Morgan's drummer, Jack Sadock, very well. He was leaving the band. And this guy was hanging around. He was writing a book with me on technical, technical, technical things. And, uh, he couldn't get a job. So, Russ Morgan, Russ Morgan needed a drummer. So, I said, I recommend it to him. They were up in Boston. So, the next morning he rings me up, Russ rings me up, he says, who is this guy? He says, your brother-in-law or your nephew? I said, what's the matter? He says, he can't play for me. He says, I fired him last night. I had to get somebody else. Lasted one night. He was showing off all over the place instead of playing drums. And that's the trouble with a lot of drummers. They want to, they want to show off more than keeping, where you take time. That was Mr. Tempo. Nick Fatool. Jack. Now, Jack's a good drummer. Jack Spurlin is a good drummer. But he's a great show off. Who do you consider the best drummer? Of the two of them? Of
Two of them? I love anyone.

All-around drummer, I think Joe Morello. Really? Joe Morello. And he's blind. When you were growing up, who did you like? There wasn't really anyone that was really my idol. Norvo has always been my idol, even when he was a xylophone player.
Oh, yeah.

And Red was, in fact, I got to know Red very well. In fact, he stayed with us here at the house. How old were you when you got to know Red? Oh, not until about 1937, when I was with Grimmer. I'll tell you who else I knew very well, who was also a great drummer. He was a studio drummer. And he had the craziest band in the world. He was a real school drummer. What the hell's his name? You know him. He had horns, cowbells on there. Oh, Spike Jones. Spike Jones. Spike Jones. I'm losing my mind. I can never remember my name, but always. Spike Jones. Spike Jones. You're good for me. Spike Jones spent... He was so surprised when he saw a Chinese crash cymbal with rivets in it. So I had to go down to one of the music stores and buy one and fix it for him, give it to him. Spike Jones.
Which drummers in this town do you remember the most strong?
Well, the only ones that I can remember...
I'm talking about when you were growing up and learning to play drums in town.

It was Paul Detrite. Paul Detrite. He was at the Orphium Theater. Uh-huh. Then Gosley. Adrian Gosley. He was always at one of the shows. Uh-huh. But Jimmy Boyle was not a good drummer. He was at the Liberty Theater. He was not a great drummer. He was a very handsome guy. He looked like Adolf Nenju. And he wore, always wore a white suit. Except at one time he was at the Liberty Theater when a rat got caught in one of the fans up there. The rat got torn to pieces and there was blood all over his white suit. Oh! Well, they had fans, big fans at their... Exhaust fans.
Exhaust fans.
I mean, fans maybe six or seven feet in diameter. And that was one thing. But they had a good band at the Liberty. They had Witt Lebowski. You heard of Witt Lebowski?
I've heard him on records, huh?

Witt Lebowski. He had a brother who was a violinist. But Witt Lebowski had a way that he could break a string on a piano. Very easily. If he was mad at you, he'd close the piano down and put his feet up on the piano like this and wouldn't touch it. They had Tony Papalia was with him down there. Jimmy Boyle. Johnny Karugi was on fiddle. And the funny thing about it, Robert Morton and Ray McNamara were the organist. And I used to stay down there at night to close, to put, I don't know if I told you, to put the trap on the organ?
For the rats.
For the rats. Do you know about that?
Yeah, you told me about that.

You told me about that. That's how I got to know Ray and Bob Morton very well. And the funny thing about it, and maybe I'm repeating myself, but when I went to the Sanger Theater, they were surprised that I read so well. You know why? Same show. It was the same music they were playing at the Liberty Theater. I knew it by heart. They were very surprised that I read so well.
You didn't pay any attention to Monk Hazel or Ash?
Yeah, I knew Monk.
I knew it. And growing up, those weren't the guys you listened to.
No, I mean, no, they were not. They were good jazz, good players. I don't say that they were Dixieland or, we had a band once at the Holland Inn. I had four drummers in it.
Four drummers? At the same time?

The Six Beasts Band, it was four drummers. We had Monk Hazel playing mellophone. Ray Benitez was playing bass. Jack Otto was playing piano. Jack Otto was playing drums. And I was playing piano, who was also a drummer. And I was the name of Colomaz, who was a alto, a tenor saxophone player. That was the band. They had four drummers. And all of them playing different instruments. I mean, Monk was playing the mellophone. Not French horn, he played mellophone.
Did you have an act?
No, it was a dance. It was a dance. Dance, nightclub.
Yeah. You didn't do anything with all the doubling.
No.
I mean, there are bands that used to do that.
No, we used to play at the famous, at the Two Bits Club. You know who owned it? The Hip Ginley was the one that owned it. Hip Ginley owned it. He was, it was at that time, he was in good.
The second reel is rolling. Take those if you want. You can make a jigsaw puzzle out of one of them if you want.
A jigsaw puzzle? That's fun.
The second reel on the 10th of November 1987. I was going to ask you about this Prima-Gonfrey orchestra.
Well, okay, we got the third reel, Godfrey Hirschhorn. Who shot off fireworks on the job? You know, you were a kid?
David Wade. Wade Schlegel.
That's what I thought.
He had his fireworks and his blank pistol. The first job that we played, I told you we had to put long pants on him.

So you were saying about the Bienville Hotel? So we went up there to play for New Year's Eve. You know how to get to the bathroom? Yeah, I found it. It's right before, right out in the little hall. Yeah. I'll go past Art Taylor.
